chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
title: Southern dance halls, spectators and tobacco warehouses
summary: Dances were mostly Black, with White spectators watching from the side; some were held in big tobacco warehouses arranged by local promoters.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Now, were most of these places that you played for Blacks, Whites, Mixed?
Most of them in the South were Black. Once in a while we'd get a White occasion. Very seldom mixed. Very seldom. Because after all, you know, this was in the Thirties.
Yeah, but I've heard those stories about the rope down the middle and all that stuff.

Oh yeah. Well, that was for the spectators. See, there would be a Black dance. Now, the Blacks would come in there and dance all over the place, one of them things. But the Whites... We'd have as many White spectators. They couldn't dance, but they could spend their

money, come in there and stand up or sit down, and they could watch the band. But they couldn't go on the floor and dance. They were what's called spectators. And there would be as many of them as there were Blacks on the floor dancing.
Well, that's what they called them down there.

Some of them were tobacco warehouses. Tobacco warehouses. Those are big places where they'd keep the tobacco. And they could accommodate a lot of people. Well, that's what they needed when you had an attraction down there, because the people would come out in droves. Yeah, they came out in droves. You needed a warehouse.
And then Glaser had arranged all this from New York.

Well, no. He just gets the dates, and whoever is promoting the dance... Whoever was promoting the dances arranged that. See, that's just like you, you hire an organization from anywhere and they come here. Well, you
know what they're going to need, this-that-and-the-other. But you see that it's there.
